final_proof:
Let the population consist of \(N\) labelled people, partitioned in advance into families. Choose a person \(I\) uniformly from the population, independently of all sexes. Write \(S_I\) for the size of \(I\)'s family and \(B_I\) for the number of \(I\)'s brothers. Interpret “half are men and half are women” in the manner compatible with the stated independence assumption: every person is male with probability \(1/2\), independently of every other person. Thus half of a large population are male approximately, rather than with deterministic exactness. Assume \(\mathbb E S_I<\infty\) if the population is allowed to be infinite or random.

Condition on \(S_I=s\). The sex of \(I\) is independent of both \(S_I\) and the sexes of the other \(s-1\) members of the family. Consequently, whether we further condition on \(I\) being female or on \(I\) being male, each of those \(s-1\) people is independently male with probability \(1/2\). Hence

\[
(B_I\mid S_I=s,\ I\text{ female})\sim\operatorname{Bin}(s-1,1/2)
\quad\text{and}\quad
(B_I\mid S_I=s,\ I\text{ male})\sim\operatorname{Bin}(s-1,1/2).
\]

Moreover, \(S_I\) has the same conditional distribution given either sex of \(I\), since sex is independent of family membership and family size. Mixing the displayed binomial law over \(S_I\) therefore proves the stronger statement

\[
(B_I\mid I\text{ female})\overset d=(B_I\mid I\text{ male}).
\]

In particular,

\[
\mathbb E[B_I\mid I\text{ female}]
=\frac12\mathbb E[S_I-1]
=\mathbb E[B_I\mid I\text{ male}].
\]

This conclusion does not require any specification of the distribution of family sizes.

There is a minor logical point concerning a literal reading of “half.” In a finite population, independent fair sexes do not imply that exactly \(N/2\) people are male. Indeed, exact equality of the two totals is not compatible with mutual independence (except in a degenerate model). If instead one starts with even \(N\) and chooses uniformly among assignments having exactly \(N/2\) males, the answer is slightly different. Conditional on \(I\) being female, any specified other person is male with probability

\[
\frac{N/2}{N-1},
\]

whereas conditional on \(I\) being male that probability is

\[
\frac{N/2-1}{N-1}.
\]

The family partition is fixed, so \(S_I\) has the same distribution under the two conditions. By linearity of expectation,

\[
\mathbb E[B_I\mid I\text{ female}]-\mathbb E[B_I\mid I\text{ male}]
=\frac{\mathbb E[S_I-1]}{N-1}.
\]

Thus women have a small expected advantage in the fixed-total model, but that model has deliberately abandoned independence of sexes. For ordinary family sizes in a large population, this finite-population correction tends to zero.

Finally, the proposed family-by-family argument confuses two differently weighted averages. If a family contains \(g\) girls and \(b\) boys, every girl in it has \(b\) brothers, while every boy has \(b-1\) brothers. But the average over all women weights this family by \(g\), whereas the average over all men weights it by \(b\). Pointwise comparison inside each family cannot compare averages having different weights.

A concrete refutation makes this decisive. Take two families, each of size \(11\): the first has one girl and ten boys, and the second has ten girls and one boy. There are exactly eleven people of each sex. In each family every girl has exactly one more brother than every boy in that same family. Nevertheless the women's average number of brothers is

\[
\frac{1\cdot10+10\cdot1}{11}=\frac{20}{11},
\]

while the men's average is

\[
\frac{10\cdot9+1\cdot0}{11}=\frac{90}{11}.
\]

So even the claimed direction can be reversed in a realized population. Under the independent fair-sex model, such imbalances occur in particular realizations but cancel in expectation, giving the exact equality proved above.
